title: Dementia Care's Hardest Part Isn't the Patient — It's the Caregiver Being Ground Down
dek: The hardest part of dementia care isn't the patient's condition itself, but the caregiver worn down day after day — caregiving turns a wife into a nurse and makes a post-90s kid quit their job; love is the starting point but not the support, and the system hasn't caught these families yet.
why: This isn't elderly-health popular science — it's the field honesty of a sociologist who walked into dementia households: no standard answers, only a reality you must see in advance.
who: Post-80s and post-90s only children, and urbanites whose parents are starting to age while they've made no eldercare arrangements at all; also for anyone who wants to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care gap will be pushed back onto every family
points.body: China has 323 million people over 60, 23% of the population; 35 million are disabled elders, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap hasn't been absorbed by the market or institutions, and the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient count is nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average one in every 20 Chinese families is affected — for the first generation of only children, this may be a reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies can't be trusted
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, the misunderstanding Tang Yong most wants to correct is this: there is no uniform image of a dementia patient. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from films, neighbors, or hearsay — the professor's incontinence in Still Alice is just one form. He has met a tailor who, after dementia, still noticed stains on visitors' clothes and taught people to remove them with orange peel; and a man disabled by a car crash who, when he could only hum Liuyang River, wore an expression of intense focus. Dementia itself covers Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, and other causes; each person's life imprint lingers in a different way, and caregiving can't be performed from a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal is paid for by state nursing insurance
points.body: Most people take the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: elders here stroll the supermarket and visit cafés like residents, while staff play shopkeepers to keep the atmosphere normal. But the details the host adds expose how hard it is to replicate — the 23 homes built in 2009 cost over 18 million euros, of which 17.8 million was borne by the government, and residents' fees are also covered by long-term care-related systems. What Tang Yong saw in a low-income American nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to keep dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease, and the difference lies not in philosophy but in the state's payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice will grind down the caregiver too
points.body: The host sums up the caregiver's predicament precisely: many people swing back and forth between ‘I love my mom and dad so much’ and ‘I'm about to be crushed by my mom and dad.’ Tang Yong says caregiving is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse has to learn to bathe, feed, and handle emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a devotion to be romanticized: a daughter he interviewed in Guangzhou twenty years ago divorced and fell into severe depression after caring for her disabled father; the book also includes a post-90s caregiver forced to quit their job under caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, the caregiver becomes a patient too.

points.h: The more you see, the less certain eldercare feels
points.body: After years of researching elder care, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his parents' old age. He is a first-generation only child, both parents are 75 this year, but the more cases he sees the less certain he feels; a research assistant even said after every interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how she would arrange things for her own parents. Multi-child families have friction too: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving gives the elder bedsores; only-child families lack people to share the load, and some who brought their parents to Shenzhen found rent, medical bills, and nanny fees stacking up faster than pensions rise. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing something every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that the caregiver must repeatedly accept loss. Volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elder who at first could paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others and not put brush to paper; another elder's husband reported new losses every week: his wife couldn't recognize the grandchild their daughter had just had, didn't know where this child had come from. This day-after-day, irreversible downward slide drains a caregiver more than physical disability. The long duration of care isn't the repetition of hardship — it's facing a small goodbye every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance is here, but it can't catch every elder
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 has spread to about 90 cities, with the official pace being universal coverage within the next two to three years. But Tang Yong cautions that long-term care insurance doesn't hand money to every elder; through unified assessment it mainly covers the moderately and severely disabled, paying for home nursing, meal delivery, and other services; the mildly impaired may not qualify. The hardest part is mindset: sending parents to a nursing home in China is often equated with unfiliality, and elders, like the grandfather in the interviews, feel that after a month there their hair is nearly falling out. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the share actively choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear on its own.

terms.def: A closed community designed for severely dementia-impaired elders, where staff play residents to maintain a normal living atmosphere.
By Arthur Kleinman, arguing that caregiving is not one-way help but a relationship.
Unpaid care provided by spouses, children, and other family members, as distinct from hired nannies and care workers.
Social insurance that pays for nursing services for disabled and dementia-impaired elders, not a cash subsidy.
Painting on wet watercolor paper so colors bleed naturally, used as non-pharmacological intervention for dementia patients.

quotes.text: I love my mom and dad so much, and I'm about to be crushed by my mom and dad — I swing back and forth between these two feelings.
So I think this caregiving is still a kind of relationship. In this relationship, the identities, emotions, and even the pace of life of both the caregiver and the cared-for change enormously.
It's like going down a slide — you're on the way down. So at that moment, I think this kind of caregiving really is long.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it shouldn't be the whole condition of caregiving. It still needs some external resources, including some social support, and so on.

Although the more I see, the more cases I come into contact with, it doesn't actually mean I have a very complete or perfect plan for my parents' old age. Precisely because I've seen so many different stories, it's actually given me more confusion.
His wife actually couldn't recognize the baby his daughter had — his little grandchild. He didn't know where this child had come from, arriving at their home.
